issues.item: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: The profile is centered on witnessed trauma with triggers involving crowded places, conversation topics, and bus riding, plus appraisals of vigilance and outsider status. The anger-loss-of-control appraisal introduces a distinct perpetration/impulse-control theme that is not supported by the other selected triggers, memory, threat, or strategy items, making it clinically hard to place within the same formulation.

Avoiding sex is not well linked to the rest of the profile. There are no sexual trauma cues, intimacy-related triggers, body-related appraisals, or threat/memory items that would explain sex-specific avoidance. Relative to the rest of the selected items, this strategy appears disconnected and inconsistent with the formulation.

vignette: Mary, a 72-year-old network engineer from North America, has been struggling with symptoms following a traumatic event. About six months ago, she witnessed her colleague collapsing and dying during a networking conference in a crowded venue. Since then, Mary finds herself increasingly anxious whenever she is in public spaces or engaged in certain conversations that remind her of the incident. Mary had come to believe that the world was an unpredictable and dangerous place, especially since witnessing such a sudden and tragic event. This constant vigilance has made it nearly impossible for her to feel safe in crowded places, such as shopping centers or bus rides. The memory of the chaos and panic she experienced during the conference triggers her belief that similar events could happen at any moment. Consequently, Mary avoids these situations entirely, staying away from public transport and large gatherings. Despite her efforts to avoid triggers, Mary found herself becoming more isolated and feeling like an outsider in both her professional and personal life. She began to force herself to think only positive thoughts when she encountered any reminders of the event, hoping that this would help her cope with her anxiety. However, these attempts at positivity often backfired, leading her to feel more anxious and out of control. One particularly distressing day, Mary had to take a bus ride home from work. The crowded conditions on the bus triggered intense feelings of dread and fear. She found herself constantly monitoring the environment around her, hyper-aware of every sound and movement. This constant vigilance made it nearly impossible for her to relax or engage in conversation with colleagues at work, as certain topics would immediately bring back memories of the traumatic event. Mary’s avoidance behaviors have had significant consequences on her daily life. She has started to miss important networking events that are crucial for her career development and has become increasingly isolated from friends and family. Her husband has noticed a change in her demeanor, noting how she avoids going out or engaging in activities they used to enjoy together. The constant vigilance and feeling of being an outsider have led Mary to believe that she is less capable of handling the world around her. This belief only reinforces her tendency to avoid situations that might trigger memories of the traumatic event. Her attempts at positive reframing have not alleviated her anxiety but rather have made her feel more out of control, exacerbating her negative appraisals. Mary’s situation has reached a point where she feels overwhelmed and helpless. The constant fear of another traumatic event occurring in public spaces has left her feeling isolated and disconnected from the world around her. It was these mounting fears and feelings of being an outsider that finally brought her to seek help, hoping for some relief from her overwhelming sense of danger and isolation. Mary is most afraid of losing control in a crowded place or during a conversation about work, where she might feel exposed or vulnerable. She hopes that through therapy, she can regain a sense of safety and reconnect with the world around her without feeling constantly on guard.
